content.content:
A listed id that names a node takes the accent focus outline while it has the focus. When the focus is on a listed entry, that entry is marked by an outline drawn in the accent colour role, so a reader can see which entry the focus rests on without moving it or trying it to find out. The outline is the whole of the mark: the entry's text stays the bare id (mwwxxzyk) and nothing is added to the entry — no element, no label, no glyph, no extra text — so the section still reports the ids its node records and the entry still says what it said. The outline is not what makes the entry a link (mwwxxzyk), and it does not stand in for the look that does.

The outline is drawn in the accent colour role recorded for focus (qqmrtwor): --vscode-focusBorder, taken as the editor's theme defines that role. This decision spends that role as it is recorded and adds no colour of its own — no literal colour value, no second token, no substitute for the accent where the theme supplies one. How thick the outline is, how far it sits from the entry and how it is shaped around the entry's box are not fixed here; what is fixed is that the entry is outlined and the recorded role the outline is drawn in.

The outline is shown while the entry has the focus and only then. It appears as the focus arrives at the entry and stops when the focus leaves it. An entry that does not have the focus carries no outline from this decision, and nothing here makes the outline a resting decoration of a listed entry or a mark that outlives the focus. Hover is not this state: an entry with the pointer over it and no focus does not take the outline, and a focused entry keeps it whether or not the pointer is over it. What a listed entry looks like on hover is a separate commitment with its own check, and nothing here describes, forbids or implies it. Nothing here says how focus arrives at an entry, where it goes when it leaves, or how many entries can hold it, and nothing here changes what activating an entry does or how activation is reached: the outline is the look of a state a listed entry can already be in.

The outline belongs to a listed entry that names a node document, in any of the four relationship sections, whether that id names a decision or an evaluation — the entries (mwwxxzyk) presents as links. It does not extend to the rest of the panel: focus resting on a section's label, on the selected node's kind, content or rationale text, or on anything on the canvas, is not marked by this decision. An id that names no node document is not this decision's case; the cues that entry takes are settled where that case is owned, and nothing here grants or withholds a focus cue for it, requires it to be marked like the entry that names a node, or requires it to differ.

This decision fills exactly the one part (mwwxxzyk) left open — what marks a listed entry while it has the focus — and leaves every other part it abstained from as it stands. It does not say which colour role the entry's text takes, whether a pointer cursor is shown over the entry, what happens to the entry on hover, which element carries the outline, or which class vocabulary names the entry or its focused state: each of those is a separate commitment with its own check, and none of them is fixed, required, forbidden or implied here. Nor does this decision add any class, style property, stylesheet rule or source of its own: it states the state a listed entry is marked in and the recorded role that mark is drawn in, and those are realised where the viewer's styles are written.
content.rationale:
A listed entry is already activatable and already reads as a link (mwwxxzyk), and the panel can be walked with the focus: the one thing such an entry has no look for is the state a reader is in while the focus is on it. Without a mark for that state a reader who arrives without a pointer cannot tell which of a column of alike entries the next activation would take, and has to try one to find out — the same gap the link look closed for the pointer. The focus indicator is the smallest commitment that makes an activation that already exists legible from the focus, and the state of a listed entry is a fact no other decision in the panel owns.

The outline takes the accent role rather than a colour of its own because the panel should mark focus the way the editor around it marks focus, and because a literal value or a second token would put a decision about the viewer's palette inside a decision about a list of ids. Spending the role as qqmrtwor records it keeps the mark on the theme's terms: the accent is the role the focus state's colour comes from, and this decision neither invents a colour nor narrows the theme to one.

Showing it only while the entry has the focus is what makes it an indicator rather than decoration. An outline that stayed after the focus left would say something false about the state of the panel, and one that appeared on hover would either double with the hover rule or replace it; keeping hover out of this decision lets the hover commitment be checked on its own terms, as a pointer state, while this one is checked as a focus state. The same restraint over which entries it covers keeps it clear of the case that is not its own: an id that names no node document is a different case with cues of its own, and an entry that cannot be followed can be marked for focus or not as that decision settles, without this one having to say so.

Stopping at the state and the role is also what keeps the commitment checkable. Whether a listed entry carries an outline while it has focus, and whether that outline resolves to the recorded role, are facts a reviewer can point at in the styles and in the running panel, so the commitment can be gated as an observable where the viewer becomes code. The remainder — the text colour role, the pointer, the hover rule, the element that draws the outline, the class vocabulary — is still unstated here, and stating any of it would either pre-empt the decision that owns it or restate what that decision says, which is exactly what mwwxxzyk's own abstentions were there to prevent.
